text:
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer scientist and engineer known for designing several innovative early computing systems. Born in Turin, Italy, into a family of intellectuals and alpinists, he joined the Polish Home Army during World War II despite being blinded by an explosion at age 14. After recovering, he returned to engineering, graduating from Warsaw University of Technology in 1951. His career breakthrough came with the construction of AKAT-1 in 1959, the world's first differential equations analyzer based on transistors, followed by the perceptron in 1964, the first such device in the Communist bloc.
In 1965, Karpiński designed KAR-65, a high-speed scientific computer that processed data from CERN bubble chambers using only domestic components. His most ambitious project was the K-202, a minicomputer built entirely with Intel 4004 chips that featured memory segmentation, floating-point arithmetic, and a speed of nearly one million operations per second. Although the K-202 was technically superior to its contemporaries, it failed to achieve mass production due to political interference, censorship, and competition from state monopolies. Karpiński later worked on tape recorders in Switzerland and returned to Poland in the 1990s to serve as an advisor to economic reformers. He died in Wrocław in 2010 and was posthumously awarded the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta.
